This model asks one question that no earlier model in the family can ask: among children with Down syndrome, does being **further ahead receptively at an earlier visit** predict converting a **larger share of comprehension into speech later**? Earlier models are not blind to conversion differences — VG09 and VG10 already give every child their own persistent production-ratio level — but none of them links a child's *earlier comprehension standing* to their later conversion: that association is exactly zero in them by construction. VG16 adds a single coefficient, $\beta$, that lets it be nonzero — and the value of $\beta$ is the whole point of the model (issue [#113](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/113), Q2).

```{python}

render_model_at_a_glance()
```

::: {.callout-important title="What is fitted here, and how to read the coefficient"}

**One model is fitted.** VG16 as registered uses the **population-relative** baseline: a child's earlier comprehension is measured against the population-and-study expectation for their age at that visit. There is one registered definition, one fit, and one trace, and everything reported on this page comes from it. A _within-child_ alternative — measuring the same child against their own estimated comprehension level instead — has been run off the record, at a lower sampling tier and with no fitted artefact in this output directory; it is discussed under [The within-child alternative](#sec-within-child) and its figures are deliberately not quoted here.

**The lag construction was corrected on 2026-08-23** ([#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242)). The previous implementation assigned lag sources row by row, so which of two same-recorded-age checklist rows carried the lag depended on arbitrary tie order and 66 spoken observations lost their lag to it. Sources are now assigned per complete child-age administration wave. Fits made before the correction — including the previously quoted `+0.203` — used a different, defective predictor and are quotable only as historical values with that provenance.

**Read $\beta$ as a history-conditioned mixture, mostly between-child.** The population-relative baseline does not subtract a child's own persistent level, so the coefficient mixes _this child is ahead of themselves today_ with _this child is generally ahead of other children_ — and it can also stand in for a persistent comprehension-conversion correlation that this model's independent child effects cannot express (VG20 estimates that correlation directly). The defensible reading is conditional: **under this model's structure and its observed measurement history, children who stood further ahead receptively at an earlier visit are expected to convert more of what they understand into speech**. VG16 alone does not establish a within-child dynamic, a causal mechanism or a causal direction, and how much of the signal is between-child versus within-child has not been separated by a purpose-built comparison. See `notes/202608231714-vg16-statistical-model-review.md` §4.1.

:::

For full details and discussion, please refer to the technical report.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Terms specific to this model"}

**Wave**

: One occasion on which a child was assessed, defined operationally as every row the child carries at one recorded age in months — a child given two checklist forms at the same recorded age contributes one wave with two rows. A child seen three times contributes three waves. The gap between waves is irregular and is not a design feature of any single study. The stored data establish the same recorded age, not necessarily simultaneous administrations, and the likelihood treats two same-wave forms as conditionally independent measurements — an assumption, not a finding.

**Cross-lag**

: A coefficient linking a quantity measured at an _earlier_ wave to a different quantity measured at a _later_ wave, over and above whatever the model already says about age and about the child. Here, earlier comprehension standing to later conversion rate.

**Cross-lagged panel model, and its random-intercept form (RI-CLPM)**

: The standard family this construction belongs to. A classic cross-lagged panel model regresses each outcome on the other's earlier value. The random-intercept form first gives every child their own persistent level for each outcome, so that the cross-lag describes deviations _from that level_ rather than the mixture of persistent and temporary differences the classic form measures. VG16's subject random intercepts are those random intercepts; whether the cross-lag on top of them reads as within-child depends on the baseline chosen for the lag predictor, which is the subject of @sec-within-child.

**Population-relative baseline** (used here)

: The lag predictor is the child's earlier comprehension minus the population-plus-study expectation at that earlier age. It does not subtract the child's own persistent level, so it carries both between-child and within-child information.

**Within-child baseline** (not fitted as a model of record)

: The same predictor with the child's own comprehension intercept subtracted as well, leaving only their temporary deviation from their own level.

**Attenuation**

: The shrinking of a fitted coefficient towards zero when its predictor is measured with noise, under the **classical** errors-in-variables model. The lag predictor here is an observed count carrying sampling noise and occasion movement, so attenuation is plausible — but the classical conditions are not established for a boundary-clipped logit of a Beta-Binomial count inside a nonlinear multilevel model, so the fitted $\beta$ is **not** a proven floor on the association with true standing. Any disattenuated figure is a heuristic sensitivity under explicit classical assumptions, not a corrected estimate.

:::

## Statistical model

The mean structure is **VG10's**, not VG09's. Words understood are a bounded count out of the reference inventory with a Beta-Binomial likelihood; on the logit scale, the expected proportion understood is a straight-line trend in age plus an _anchored_ Gaussian process, plus a study offset and a child offset:

$$f_U(a, s, i) = \text{intercept}_U + \text{slope}_U \cdot a_z + \tilde g_U(a) + \delta_U[s] + \delta^{\text{subj}}_U[i]$$

Here $a_z$ is standardised age, $\delta_U[s]$ is the offset of study $s$, $\delta^{\text{subj}}_U[i]$ the persistent offset of child $i$, and $\tilde g_U$ the anchored Gaussian process. The expected proportion of the reference inventory a child understands is $p_U = \operatorname{logit}^{-1} f_U$. This equation matters more here than in any other report in the family, because the lag predictor below is defined against it.

Spoken words are modelled _through_ comprehension. Where a row carries both counts and they are logically nested, spoken words are drawn conditionally on that child's own observed understood count, $S \mid U \sim \operatorname{BetaBinomial}(U, q, \kappa_S)$; a row with no usable understood count falls back to the marginal form against the full reference inventory. The production ratio has the same shape as the understood trajectory, plus the cross-lag:

$$h(a, s, i) = \text{intercept}_q + \text{slope}_q \cdot a_z + \tilde g_q(a) + \delta_q[s] + \delta^{\text{subj}}_q[i] + \beta\, x^{\text{lag}}_i$$

with $q = \operatorname{logit}^{-1} h$ and $p_S = p_U \, q$. The likelihood's $q$ is the _child's_ ratio, including both random effects and the lag term — not the population curve plotted later on this page.

### The anchored geometry {#sec-anchor}

VG16 was originally specified as "VG09 plus a cross-lag" and so inherited VG09's _unanchored_ Gaussian processes. That made it the worst-behaved model in the family: it produced by far the most divergent transitions of any model with subject random effects, and its worst R-hat was far outside the publication gate. It was moved onto **VG10's anchored geometry**, and this fit uses that.

The problem the anchor solves is redundancy. A Gaussian process free to take any smooth shape can imitate the straight-line trend — a draw can raise the line and lower the process by the same amount, or tilt one against the other — and the data cannot separate them. On every posterior draw the unit-amplitude process is therefore least-squares projected out of the directions the mean already spans, both the constant and the linear-in-age direction, using the observed rows only; the residual is then shifted to be exactly zero at the reference age. Removing the constant fixes the process's level against the intercept; removing the linear direction is what stops it trading off against the slope, and that is the part that actually resolved the geometry. The reference age is in the glance box above.

### Levelling the production ratio off above the high anchor {#sec-clamp}

Above the high age anchor, the production ratio's mean is held level rather than extrapolated along its line; the understood mean is not. Continued upward on the logit scale the $q$ line runs to near-saturation past the data, and the flexible term then spends its budget correcting that asymptote instead of describing the ages where observations are. The corner is rounded so the curve stays smooth and monotone. For a reader this matters only at the oldest reported ages: the visible levelling-off in the production-ratio figure is this constraint, not a discovery about vocabulary.

The reporting caps in the glance box differ by outcome for a related reason. Comprehension is recorded on fewer rows and thins out earlier in age, so its reporting cap sits below the high trend anchor — at the age where the data stop determining the answer rather than where they stop existing — and every ratio built from understood inherits the narrower cap. Only the production ratio's mean is levelled above the anchor; the understood mean is not. That is why the two lines in the joint-trajectory figures stop at different ages.

### The cross-lag {#sec-crosslag-def}

For each observation of a child who has an **earlier** observed wave with a usable understood count, at age $a_{\text{prev}}$:

$$x^{\text{lag}}_i = \operatorname{logit}\!\big(\text{understood}_{\text{prev}}/N\big) - \big(f_U(a_{\text{prev}}) + \delta_U[s]\big)$$

where $N$ is the reference inventory. In words: **how far above or below the population-and-study expectation for their age that child's comprehension stood at their previous visit**, on the logit scale. The subtracted term is the population trajectory plus the study offset — and _not_ the child's own offset $\delta^{\text{subj}}_U[i]$, which is what makes this the population-relative baseline rather than the within-child one.

The unit is the **administration wave** defined in the glossary: every row a child carries at one recorded age, processed as a complete group ([#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242)). Every row in a wave receives the same source — the child's most recent strictly earlier wave with a usable understood count, skipping earlier waves without one — and the source state advances only once the whole wave is assigned, so the construction is invariant to the order rows happen to arrive in. Where a source wave carries understood counts from two checklist forms, the larger count is selected, being the least-truncated available measurement on the shared inventory; no wave in the current frame yet exercises that rule. $x^{\text{lag}}$ is zero where there is no earlier usable wave: a child's first wave, or a child whose every earlier wave lacks comprehension. The coefficient is therefore identified only by observations that carry both a usable prior wave and a spoken count in the likelihood — a minority of the fitted frame, counted below.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

import pandas as _pd

if _os.path.isfile("cross_lag_audit.csv"):

    _audit["spoken_branch"] = _audit["spoken_branch"].fillna("")
    _support = _audit[_audit["spoken_branch"] != ""]
    _gaps = _support["gap_months"]
    _ceiling_changes = (
        int(_support["form_ceiling_changed"].sum())
        if "form_ceiling_changed" in _support.columns
        else None

    print(
        f"**The lag support, read from this fit's own `cross_lag_audit.csv`.** "
        f"{len(_audit)} observations carry a prior-wave understood source; "
        f"**{len(_support)}** of them also carry a spoken count in the likelihood and so "
        f"identify $\\beta$, contributed by **{_support['subject_code'].nunique()} children** "
        f"({int((_support['spoken_branch'] == 'conditional').sum())} on the conditional "
        f"$S \\mid U$ branch, {int((_support['spoken_branch'] == 'marginal').sum())} on the "
        f"marginal fallback). Gaps between the source and current waves run "
        f"{_gaps.min():.0f}–{_gaps.max():.0f} months (median {_gaps.median():.0f}, IQR "
        f"{_gaps.quantile(0.25):.0f}–{_gaps.quantile(0.75):.0f}), and one constant "
        f"coefficient averages over that whole range. "
        f"{int(_support['source_understood_zero'].sum())} supporting sources have an "
        f"understood count of zero, entering through a clipped logit."
        + (
            f" {_ceiling_changes} supporting rows change checklist-form ceiling between "

            if _ceiling_changes is not None
            else ""
        )

    print()
    print(
        "Gap-restricted, gap-interaction, same-form and boundary-treatment "

```

Because the model already gives every child a persistent production-ratio offset $\delta^{\text{subj}}_q[i]$, $\beta$ is not simply picking up "some children talk more". It is a shift in conversion associated with earlier _comprehension_ standing, on top of each child's own stable conversion level.

### Hierarchy

Study offsets are constrained to sum to zero, so the population curve is the average study rather than an arbitrary reference. Child offsets are ordinary random intercepts on both the understood trajectory and the production ratio. All four blocks use the non-centred form $\delta = \tau z$.

## Priors

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
from vocab_growth.report_cells import render_priors_table

render_priors_table()
```

The trajectory, hierarchy and dispersion priors are inherited unchanged from the Down syndrome joint lineage; see VG10's report for their provenance. Two points are specific to this model.

**The cross-lag prior is centred on zero and symmetric.** The direction is not baked in: a negative coefficient is exactly as probable _a priori_ as a positive one of the same size, so a posterior that excludes zero is the data speaking rather than the prior. Its scale is stated on the logit scale, per unit of the lag predictor, and the predictor's own unit is a logit of comprehension relative to expectation — so the prior scale is large enough to permit shifts in conversion far bigger than anything the trajectories exhibit, and it constrains the answer only by ruling out the absurd.

**The high production-ratio anchor and both understood anchors are frame calibration**, not independent norms: they were set so the prior trend line sits where the directly observed comprehension and spoken/understood ratios sit, because no external norm exists for either quantity in Down syndrome. The low production-ratio anchor is centred on an independent typically-developing estimate. None of them is read off a model's posterior.

Both dispersion blocks use the two-anchor form, with priors stated as $\kappa$ at two reference ages rather than as an intercept and a slope. These $\kappa$ are conditional: with study and child random intercepts in the model, $\kappa$ describes what is left once a child's own level is known.

## Prior predictive checks

These simulate vocabularies from the priors alone, before the data are seen. The criteria are the family's: young children should usually sit near the floor on both outcomes, older trajectories should not be forced towards the ceiling, and the production ratio should be free to take both low and high values across the age range. The figures below meet them — the prior envelopes stay wide at every age and neither outcome is pinned.

![Trajectories for words understood drawn from the priors alone.](prior_samples_u.png){#fig-prior-samples-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Trajectories for words spoken drawn from the priors alone.](prior_samples_s.png){#fig-prior-samples-s .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![Trajectories for the production ratio $q(a)$ drawn from the priors alone.](prior_samples_q.png){#fig-prior-samples-q .lightbox fig-align="left"}

::: {.callout-note title="One prior check this fit still does not carry"}

The three figures above are the shared trajectory draws; none of them isolates the cross-lag term. The coefficient's own prior is now plotted under [Priors](#cross-lag-coefficient) so it can be read against its posterior, but the scoping note's fuller requirement — the prior translated into production-ratio shifts over the empirical range of the lag predictor, plus a prior-scale sensitivity on the corrected fit — remains registered follow-up work in [#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242). Until it exists, a posterior that excludes zero should be read alongside the symmetric prior figure, not treated as prior-independent.

:::

## Data

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

descriptive_stats = pd.read_csv("descriptive_statistics.csv", index_col=0)
descriptive_stats
```

The pool is the same aggregated Down syndrome frame the rest of the family uses, with per-study row counts in this fit's `fit_manifest.json`; the glance box above gives the frame size and the number of rows carrying each outcome.

What this table cannot show is the structure that identifies the cross-lag. The panel is **short and irregular**: a large share of children appear only once and contribute nothing to $\beta$, and among those seen more than once the number of visits and the gaps between them vary considerably — this is an aggregation of studies with different follow-up designs, not a single cohort on a fixed schedule. The design consequence is that $\beta$ must be extracted as one population coefficient from many short series rather than estimated from long per-child series. The counts that quantify this are stated in @sec-crosslag-def, read from this fit's own `cross_lag_audit.csv`. One further structural fact matters: the lag is active only where an earlier understood count and a later spoken count both happen to be observed, and understood missingness is partly structural — some checklist forms simply do not measure comprehension — so identification rests on that observation pattern being ignorable given the modelled study, age and child structure, an assumption the registered complete-pair and form-restricted checks in [#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242) exist to probe.

::: {.callout-note}

The normality tests in this table are reported for completeness. They are not a check on the model: the outcome is a bounded count, which is not expected to be normally distributed, and the model does not assume that it is.

:::

This project requires R-hat no greater than 1.01 and ESS of at least 400 for **every** parameter before a fit may be reported at all, so a fit reaching this page has already cleared those thresholds — or carries a recorded exception, disclosed above.

Three blocks. First `beta_lag` itself — its ESS and R-hat in the table above are the licence for everything in the next section. Second the two child scales `tau_subj_u` and `tau_subj_q`, and the two study scales `tau_u` and `tau_q`: these compete with the cross-lag for the same variation, and the pair plot's grid is deliberately ordered so that the coefficient and these scales are the parameters it shows ([#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242) — under the default model-order selection `beta_lag` fell off the end of the capped grid, so the earlier caption promised a trade-off the figure could not display). Third the production-ratio geometry — `eta_q`, `ell_unit_q` and the two $q$ anchors — which is what the anchoring described in @sec-anchor was introduced to clean up; under VG09's unanchored form this model did not sample acceptably at all.

:::

## Findings

### The cross-lag coefficient

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import pandas as _pd

_diagnostics = _pd.read_csv("diagnostics.csv", index_col=0)
if "beta_lag" in _diagnostics.index:
    _row = _diagnostics.loc["beta_lag"]
    print("| Quantity | Posterior mean | SD | 89% ETI | ESS (bulk) | R-hat |")
    print("| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |")
    print(
        f"| Cross-lag coefficient $\\beta$ (`beta_lag`) | {_row['mean']:.3f} | "
        f"{_row['sd']:.3f} | {_row['eti89_lb']:.3f} to {_row['eti89_ub']:.3f} | "
        f"{_row['ess_bulk']:,.0f} | {_row['r_hat']:.3f} |"
    )
    print()
    if _row["eti89_lb"] > 0:
        _verdict = "lies entirely **above** zero"
    elif _row["eti89_ub"] < 0:
        _verdict = "lies entirely **below** zero"
    else:
        _verdict = "**spans** zero"
    print(
        f": Read at render time from this fit's own `diagnostics.csv`, so it cannot "
        f"drift from the model it describes. The 89% equal-tailed interval {_verdict}. "
        f"The coefficient is on the logit scale of the production ratio, per unit of "
        f"the lag predictor defined in @sec-crosslag-def."
    )
else:
    print("_This fit's `diagnostics.csv` carries no `beta_lag` row._")
```

**This is the number the model exists to produce.** The interval above is the thing to quote, and the direction it excludes — or fails to exclude — is the finding. Where the interval sits entirely above zero, the reading is model-conditioned: under this structure and its observed measurement history, children who stood further ahead receptively at an earlier visit are expected to convert a larger fraction of their comprehension into speech. It is a **prospective association, not an established temporal direction**: the predictor retains persistent between-child standing, so the same posterior is compatible with a stable trait correlation that merely becomes visible wherever the study design happened to record a prior visit — which is what VG20 estimates directly. Under every model before VG16 this association is exactly zero by construction.

Three qualifications belong with it.

**It is an association, not an effect.** Nothing here says that raising a child's comprehension would produce the conversion gain. Articulation, expressive-language ability, exposure feeding both sides, or reporting tendency are all compatible with the same coefficient.

**Its measurement error has no proven direction of bias.** The lag predictor is an observed count carrying sampling noise and occasion-to-occasion movement, so classical attenuation towards zero is plausible — but the classical conditions are not established for a clipped logit of a Beta-Binomial count in this nonlinear multilevel model, so the fitted value must not be quoted as a proven **floor** on the association with true standing, and no disattenuated figure should be quoted as a corrected estimate. The heuristic calculation and its assumptions are in `notes/202608151120-vg16-cross-lag-quantified.md` §5, which is how any use of it must be framed.

**It is small relative to what it sits beside.** The variation table below is the comparison to make: the persistent between-child spread in conversion is far larger than anything the cross-lag moves, and fitting the cross-lag leaves that spread essentially untouched. The model gains a direction of prediction, not an explanation of why children differ.

### What the coefficient means, in units

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example"}

Take two children of the same age, seen at a previous visit some months earlier. At that earlier visit, child **A**'s comprehension sat exactly at the population-and-study expectation for their age; child **B**'s sat one _between-child standard deviation_ above it. What does the model expect about how much of their comprehension each says now?

1. **Get the step size.** Read the between-child standard deviation for understood — the `tau_subj_u` row — from the variation table below. It is in logits.
2. **Multiply by $\beta$.** From the table above. The product is how much higher the **logit** of child B's production ratio is than child A's, on account of the cross-lag alone.
3. **Convert to a rate.** Find the population production ratio at the current age in the [Production ratio](#sec-production-ratio) table below, take its logit, add the shift from step 2, and convert back. The difference between the two ratios is the difference in the fraction of understood words spoken.
4. **Convert to words.** Multiply each ratio by the number of words the child understands. The difference is the extra words spoken that the cross-lag accounts for.

Two things that step deliberately leaves out. Child B almost certainly also _understands_ more words than child A, so their spoken advantage has two sources: a bigger store of words, and a better conversion rate. The cross-lag is only the second. And because $q$ approaches its ceiling at older ages, the same $\beta$ buys fewer extra words the older the children are — a ceiling effect, not evidence that the association weakens.

The full decomposition of a spoken-vocabulary gap into those two channels, worked at several ages with intervals, is in `notes/202608151120-vg16-cross-lag-quantified.md` §4.

:::

Both child scales exceed both study scales, so the differences this model describes are between children rather than artefacts of pooling studies with different recruitment. The child scale on the production ratio exceeds the child scale on comprehension: children of the same age differ _more_ in how much of their comprehension they speak than in how much they comprehend. That persistent difference in conversion is the backdrop against which the cross-lag should be judged — it is what $\beta$ adds to, and what it conspicuously fails to explain away.

## The within-child alternative {#sec-within-child}

::: {.callout-important title="Withdrawn: an earlier negative within-child figure, and its explanation"}

An earlier version of this report carried a **strongly negative** within-child coefficient and attributed it to a short-panel (Nickell-type) errors-in-variables artefact — the idea that regressing on a lag defined against a child's own _estimated_ intercept induces a spurious negative association when children contribute few waves. **Both the figure and its attribution are withdrawn.**

The figure was an artefact of under-convergence at the lowest sampling tier. Refitting the same within-child baseline to the same data at a higher tier gives a _positive_ coefficient with no divergent transitions, agreeing in sign with the population-relative headline and smaller than it, with an interval that includes zero.

The attributed mechanism was then independently ruled out by simulation from this model's own posterior on the real observed wave structure: at a known coefficient of zero no estimator returns a negative value, and a variant supplied with each child's _true_ intercept agrees throughout with the variant that estimates it — so errors in the estimated intercept are not the cause. See [`202608151500`](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/blob/main/notes/202608151500-within-child-crosslag-feasibility.md) §§6–7.

**Consequences for how this report reads.** The population-relative baseline is _not_ headlined because it is robust to a bias that has been demonstrated — no such bias has been demonstrated. It is headlined for one reason that survives: it does not condition the predictor on an estimated per-child quantity. What it declines to do is isolate the within-child signal, and the strength of that signal is **undetermined, not negligible**: the off-record within-child interval includes zero *and* positive values larger than the population-relative headline, and no equivalence margin or region of practical equivalence was ever defined against which "negligible" could be claimed. Failure to establish a nonzero within-child effect is not evidence that the effect is absent.

:::

No within-child fit is a model of record. There is one registered definition and one trace, and the within-child figures referred to above come from an off-record experiment script run at a lower sampling tier with no artefact in this output directory. They are not quoted numerically here for that reason, and they should not be quoted as estimates anywhere: the correct summary of that contrast is "positive-signed, imprecise, not distinguishable from zero — and not shown to be negligible". Registering the within-child baseline as a real sensitivity variant, fitting it at reporting quality and reporting the posterior probability inside a pre-specified negligible-effect interval would make the contrast quotable; that has not been done.

One further caution on the contrast itself. In one simulation with a known within-child truth, estimating the within-child coefficient jointly with the rest of the model inflated it. That is a caution against quoting the off-record figure as an estimate — but it is a different parameterisation from the registered model, so it establishes neither the direction of bias in the headline estimator nor anything about whether the within-child effect is real, and it does not convert the interval's failure to exclude zero into evidence of absence.

## Posterior predictions

::: {.callout-important title="Which estimand each figure shows — and the conditioning they all share"}

- A **population-level** curve sets every random effect and the lag term to zero: the average child in the average study, with the interval reflecting uncertainty in that average. In the summary tables these are the `p_population_*` and `Ey_population_*` columns.
- A **subject-marginal** prediction draws a new child's random effects too, answering _where would one more child fall?_ These are the `p_subject_marginal_*` / `Ey_subject_marginal_*` columns and the `Y_*` and `P(Y<=k)` columns.

**Every prediction on this page is a zero-lag reference** ([#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242)): the grids set $x^{\text{lag}} = 0$, which is the model's own prediction for a child with **no usable lag history** — a first or only assessment, exactly the situation of most children in the frame. They are *not* marginal draws over histories from VG16's sequential data-generating process: a full longitudinal prediction would have to assume a visit schedule, simulate the earlier comprehension count and form the lag it implies, and no figure here does that. For a child known to have stood above or below expectation at an earlier visit, the model predicts a shifted production ratio these tables do not show — the worked example under [Findings](#what-the-coefficient-means-in-units) is how to add that shift by hand.

The joint-trajectory figures below are **subject-marginal**; the production-ratio and understood-versus-spoken figures are **population-level** except where a caption says predictive. Each figure states which.

:::

### Joint trajectory

![Words understood and words spoken against age, as **subject-marginal** predictive counts: the band is where individual children fall, not uncertainty in the average. The understood line stops before the spoken line for the reasons in @sec-clamp.](joint_trajectory.png){#fig-joint-trajectory .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same subject-marginal predictive trajectories with an inner 50% and an outer 89% equal-tailed interval on each outcome.](joint_trajectory_intervals.png){#fig-joint-trajectory-intervals .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Conclude that the two curves separate early and stay separated across the whole reported range, and that the outer bands are wide enough that a child well inside one is unremarkable.

### Production ratio {#sec-production-ratio}

The production ratio $q(a) = p_S(a)/p_U(a)$ is the fraction of understood words expected also to be spoken at age $a$ — the expected number of words spoken per word understood. A value of one half means half of the words a child understands are words they also say. **This is the scale $\beta$ lives on**: the cross-lag shifts the logit of this quantity.

![The population-level production ratio against age, with uncertainty intervals. It rises across the reported range: older children say a larger share of what they understand. The flattening at the top is the levelling-off described in @sec-clamp, not a finding.](production_rate.png){#fig-production-rate .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The same population-level ratio plotted against expected words understood rather than against age. Both curves are functions of age alone with the lag at zero, so this figure re-expresses the age axis — it does **not** display the cross-lag association, and it compares no same-age children at different comprehension levels. The upward bend says only that comprehension and conversion both rise with age.](production_rate_by_understood.png){#fig-production-rate-by-understood .lightbox fig-align="left"}

## Posterior predictions -- words understood

$p$ is the latent proportion of the reference inventory a child is expected to understand; $Ey$ the expected count it implies; $Y$ a draw from the posterior predictive distribution. Read the `*_population_*` columns for the average child in the average study and the `*_subject_marginal_*` and `Y_*` columns for a single unseen child — the latter are much the wider, and are the ones to quote about an individual.

```{python}
posterior_summary_u = pd.read_csv("posterior_summary_u.csv")
posterior_summary_u
```

![Median predicted words understood with uncertainty intervals, against the observed data.](posterior_predictive_median_trend_u.png){#fig-trend-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![The probability of a given understood-word count **or fewer** for a new, unseen child. Read this for questions of the form "what fraction of children understand 100 words or fewer at this age?"](posterior_predictive_cdf_u.png){#fig-cdf-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

![How the understood dispersion parameter changes with age, with uncertainty intervals.](posterior_kappa_u.png){#fig-kappa-u .lightbox fig-align="left"}

Lower $\kappa$ means **greater** between-child variability relative to the mean; higher means less. Read this as _falling $\kappa$ = children becoming more spread out_, and conclude that residual spread grows with age even after each child's own level is accounted for. Dispersion is also why the cross-lag's predictor is noisy: a comprehension count at an earlier wave is a single draw from a distribution this wide, which is why its measurement error matters for reading $\beta$ (see [Findings](#the-cross-lag-coefficient)).

## Out-of-sample prediction

::: {.callout-important title="What leave-one-out can and cannot mean for this model"}

The cross-lag makes earlier observed understood counts part of later spoken predictors, and that breaks the usual reading of pointwise leave-one-out. **Understood LOO is not computed for this model** ([#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242)): leaving an understood observation's likelihood term out does not remove that count from the later spoken terms it predicts through $x^{\text{lag}}$, so the score would still condition on the held-out outcome — and the Pareto-$k$ diagnostic checks the importance-sampling approximation, not this leakage, so it cannot flag it. The spoken score below is prediction of a spoken count **conditional on the child's observed understood history** (and, on the conditional branch, the same administration's understood count). That is a defined and useful target, but it is not unconditional new-observation prediction, and it is not comparable with the two-outcome totals other models report. A grouped forward-chaining or held-out-child sequential score is the registered replacement.

:::

```{python}

#| output: asis

render_loo_section()
```


## Limits

- **Not causal, not an intervention estimate, and not an established temporal direction.** The cross-lag is a prospective association under this model's structure and measurement history. It does not license the claim that raising comprehension would produce the conversion gain, and it does not by itself establish that earlier comprehension drives later conversion rather than both expressing a stable trait correlation.
- **A mixture, not a within-child effect.** The population-relative baseline does not isolate a child's own temporary deviation, so $\beta$ blends between-child standing with within-child movement — and can proxy a persistent comprehension-conversion correlation the independent child effects cannot express. How much is within-child is **undetermined**: the off-record within-child interval includes zero and values larger than the headline, and no equivalence bound was defined.
- **Measurement error in the predictor has no proven direction of bias here.** Classical attenuation towards zero is plausible but its conditions are not established for this clipped, heteroscedastic predictor in a nonlinear multilevel model. The fitted value is neither a proven floor nor a corrected estimate of the association with true standing.
- **A persistent link remains that this model cannot express.** With the cross-lag fitted, the realised understood and production-ratio child effects still correlate. The two random-effect blocks have independent priors and no correlation parameter, so the model has nowhere else to put that association — the correlated random-effect structure that expresses it directly is [VG20](../vg20/index.qmd), and a correlated-random-effects-plus-lag comparison is registered in [#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242).
- **Only one baseline is a model of record.** The within-child contrast is off-record and lower-tier; nothing on this page should be read as a reporting-quality within-child estimate.
- **One constant coefficient averages over heterogeneous gaps, studies and checklist-form transitions.** The audited gaps run from 1 to 28 months with no gap interaction or decay, so the estimate is a design-weighted average over this frame's particular interval distribution, not a general earlier-to-later parameter; some supporting rows also change checklist form between the source and current waves, a transition the study intercepts cannot absorb. Gap, leave-one-study-out, same-form and boundary sensitivities are registered but not yet fitted.
- **Identification rests on an available-case assumption** (@sec-crosslag-def): the lag is active only where an earlier understood count and a later spoken count are both observed, and understood missingness is partly structural because some forms do not measure comprehension. The supporting subset is a minority of the frame; every statement about $\beta$ rests on it.
- **Wave-sequential validation and recovery do not exist yet.** The generic recovery harness cannot simulate this model (its predictor is a function of the outcome), understood LOO is suppressed for the reason above, and no purpose-built sequential score or positive-truth recovery has been run — both are gates in [#242](https://github.com/dseinternational/vocabulary-growth/issues/242).
- **Beyond the high anchor the production ratio does not extrapolate — it is held level** (@sec-clamp), so quantities at the very top of the reported range are a levelled-off mean moved by the flexible term alone.
- **The reference inventory is a harmonisation.** Counts from different checklists are placed on a common scale; it is a unit of measurement, not an instrument any child sat. The lag inherits it: every prior count enters as a logit against the same 810-word inventory, an assumption the registered same-form and DSE-native sensitivities exist to probe.
